title: Vermentino
description: Also called Rolle in Provence and Pigato in Liguria. A crisp, herbal, saline white of Mediterranean coasts and islands.
L: Vermentino gives light to medium-bodied whites with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, white flowers, Mediterranean herbs and a saline, almond finish. Acidity is medium to high. It's at home by the sea, and its salty, herbal character is often linked to coastal winds and soils.

Vermentino probably spread around the western Mediterranean centuries ago. It's called Rolle in Provence and the Languedoc, Pigato in Liguria and Favorita in Piedmont; DNA shows they're the same grape. It likes heat, sun and drought, and tolerates poor, sandy or granite soils, typical of Mediterranean coasts.

Look for pale lemon colour, citrus and herbs like rosemary and thyme, a crisp palate and a slightly bitter, saline almond finish. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's less pungent and green; compared with Pinot Grigio, more herbal and saline.

Sardinia is Vermentino's stronghold. Vermentino di Gallura, in the granite north-east, is the island's only DOCG, since 1996, giving fuller, more structured, saline wines. Vermentino di Sardegna DOC covers the whole island. In Corsica, Vermentino, also called Vermentinu, makes Patrimonio and Ajaccio whites.

Tuscany's coast, Bolgheri and the Maremma, makes fresh Vermentino. Liguria's Cinque Terre and Riviera Ligure di Ponente use it and Pigato. In Provence, Rolle is the main white grape and is often blended into rosé to add freshness and aroma. Australia is planting it as a heat-tolerant grape.

Vermentino suits seafood and Mediterranean food: grilled fish, shellfish, fritto misto, pasta with clams, and pesto, Liguria's basil sauce. Its herbal notes echo basil, rosemary and thyme. Its saline edge suits oysters and anchovies.
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Most Vermentino is best within two years. Vermentino di Gallura Superiore and some oaked versions can age three to five years, gaining honey and almond notes.
